data.title: ADP 1Q 2027: Revenue $5.49B, EPS $2.83— 10-Q Summary
data.description:
Automatic Data Processing reported first-quarter fiscal 2027 revenue of $5.49 billion, up 6% from a year earlier. Net income rose 11% to $1.13 billion, while diluted earnings per share increased 14% to $2.83.

Financial Highlights

  • Revenue was $5.49B, compared with $5.18B in the prior-year quarter; YoY change 6%.
  • Net income was $1.13B, compared with $1.01B in the prior-year quarter; YoY change 11%.
  • Diluted EPS was $2.83, compared with $2.49 in the prior-year quarter; YoY change 14%.

Business Highlights

  • Organic constant-currency revenue growth was 6%, supported by new business, client retention, pricing and client-fund interest.
  • Employer Services revenue increased 6%. PEO Services revenue grew 7%, including 4% growth excluding zero-margin benefits pass-throughs.
  • ADP Assist reached more than 100,000 additional clients during the quarter, as ADP expanded AI agents across HR and talent workflows.
  • ADP Lyric HCM became available to companies headquartered in the U.K., France, Germany and the Netherlands.
  • U.S. pays per control grew 2%, and PEO average worksite employees increased 2% year over year.

Original SEC Filing: AUTOMATIC DATA PROCESSING INC [ ADP ] - 10-Q - Oct. 30, 2026

data.title: Stock Market Today: Deepening Tech Selloff Pushes Nasdaq Toward Its Worst Month in Over a Year — WSJ
data.description:
By Ed Ballard

The tech selloff is intensifying after results from Amazon and Intel compounded worries around the artificial intelligence trade.

The Nasdaq composite slumped more than 3%, while the S&P 500 lost 2.2% and the Dow industrials retreated more than 1%, or 630 points. For the tech-heavy Nasdaq, the selloff of the past two days has set the index up for its worst month since March 2025 and put it about 8.5% below its record high.

Shares of Amazon dropped about 2%; its earnings were in line with the company's forecasts-and showed booming cloud-computing growth-but left the market wanting more. Intel shares, meanwhile, are having their worst day ever, down 30% after the memory-chip crunch and other hiccups weighed on PC sales.

The AI worry comes with a side order of crypto angst in the wake of a massive cyberattack on Binance. Bitcoin and other cryptocurrencies are trading lower after hackers made off with an estimated $6.3 billion from an attack on the crypto exchange. Binance suspended transactions and said users will be made whole.

Meanwhile, oil is up after more strikes in the Middle East and Russia. Brent crude climbed to about $113 after a tanker transiting the Strait of Hormuz came under attack, according to U.K. Maritime Trade Operations. Ukraine struck an oil refinery in Russia, ending a pause that the Trump administration had pushed for.

This item is part of a Wall Street Journal live coverage event. The full stream can be found by searching P/WSJL (WSJ Live Coverage).

data.title: US SEC's top cop says agency is monitoring AI corporate disclosures
data.description:
By Chris Prentice

The US Securities and Exchange Commission is examining artificial intelligence companies' corporate disclosures as investor worries mount over a potential AI bubble that may have been fueled by circular deals, the agency's enforcement director told Reuters on Friday.

Big Tech stocks sold off this week as companies disclosed they are burning through cash to fuel their AI expansion at a time when interest rates are rising, raising questions about the sustainability of AI spending.

David Woodcock, who became SEC enforcement director in May, said the agency does not want to stand in the way of tech innovation, but that it is the agency's job to ensure issuers are giving investors the full picture on potential risks.

"Our principal concern is that people are making accurate disclosures about material information so that investors know what they're getting into," Woodcock said in an interview. "Enforcement is a very necessary piece of making sure people are doing that."

Where such disclosure does not happen, "then enforcement will be present," he said.

Woodcock also said that AI and superintelligence have made scams much easier and cheaper to manufacture at scale, raising risks for more and more people. Brokers and other firms need to have processes in place to protect retail investors and "take thoughtful action," he said.

PRIVATE MARKETS AND PREDICTION MARKETS

Woodcock said the SEC will continue to look at issues in private markets, adding that the enforcement team's asset management unit is very focused on conflicts of interest and valuations.

"When people don't make accurate disclosures, whether it's about valuations or whatever, then there is a role for enforcement," Woodcock said. "I think you'll see more activity in this space."

Reuters previously reported the SEC was probing a type of private equity fund as part of the agency's broader interest in the opaque markets.

Woodcock said the SEC also has a role in overseeing prediction markets, which allow people to bet on real-world events, including sports, government policy announcements and elections.

The markets, led by Polymarket and Kalshi, have surged in popularity over the past two years and have been pushing into US stocks. Such equity-linked prediction markets would traditionally fall under SEC jurisdiction.

Woodcock said the agency's enforcement staff are working with policy officials as well as the Commodity Futures Trading Commission, which broadly oversees swap markets, to monitor and regulate the booming new markets.

When asked about the possibility of bringing cases against firms that do not register with the agency, Woodcock said the agency does not want to regulate the new industry through enforcement actions.

"We want to be involved where it makes sense, but not in a way that crushes innovation," he said.

data.title: Govt names 1993-batch IAS officer Poundrik as heavy industries secretary
data.description:
NEW DELHI, Oct. 30 -- The appointments committee of the cabinet on Friday named 1993-batch Indian Administrative Service (IAS) officer Sandeep Poundrik as secretary of the ministry of heavy industries, according to an official order.

Poundrik, an IAS officer of the Bihar cadre, has been given additional charge of the heavy industries ministry while continuing as secretary of the steel ministry.

Union minister HD Kumaraswamy holds both the steel and heavy industries portfolios, and Poundrik's new responsibility means he will now head both ministries at the secretary level.

Poundrik's appointment comes at a time when crucial tasks for the heavy industries ministry would be to ensure smooth continuation of key electric mobility schemes such as the Rs.25,938-crore production-linked incentive scheme for automobiles and auto parts (PLI Auto) and the Rs.11,900-crore PM E-Drive scheme, while also ensuring that crucial advanced chemistry cell projects under the Rs.18,100-crore PLI scheme for advanced chemistry cells (PLI ACC) scheme takes off successfully.

The ministry also oversees operations at state-run Bharat Heavy Electricals Ltd (Bhel), an integral engineering and infrastructure sector public enterprise, which makes power generation equipment, transportation and railway equipment, defence and aerospace sector manufacturing, and clean energy products.

The ministry is also responsible for running the Rs.1,207 crore Scheme for Enhancement of Competitiveness in the Indian Capital Goods Sector - Phase II, under which the government runs industry accelerators and skilling programmes to reduce gaps in research and development in the capital goods sector.

In November 2025, the heavy industries ministry also launched a Rs.7,280-crore incentive package to set up five rare earth magnet making plants in the country, in the wake of a global rare earth magnet shortage caused by Chinese export controls in retaliation to steep US tariffs.

Rare earth magnets are made from monazite deposits, of which India is the world's third largest source. These magnets are made after processing monazite --- China controls around 60% of the world's rare earth mining and 90% of the world's rare earth processing capacity --- and these magnets are used in crucial manufacturing sectors such as defence, electronics, renewable energy, and automobiles including cleaner electric vehicles.

The PLI Auto and PLI ACC schemes, along with the PM E-Drive and the rare earth magnet making scheme, are crucial for advancing India's progress towards meeting the country's target of becoming a net-zero carbon emitter by 2070.

The government has supported the rollout of 1.1 million electric vehicles - 811,357 electric two-wheelers, 2,168 e-rickshaws (L3 category), 288,508 electric three-wheelers (L5 category), and 155 electric trucks - under the PM E-Drive scheme. The government has also sanctioned 14,000 e-buses under the scheme, through tenders issued by Convergence Energy Services Ltd (CESL).

Under the PLI Auto scheme, the government has disbursed Rs.2,386.86 crore by the end of FY26, with the scheme set to disburse incentives for manufacturing zero-emission vehicles till FY29. Currently, eight vehicle makers and 10 component makers are eligible to claim incentives under this scheme.

The PLI ACC scheme, which targets setting up of 50 GWh cell making capacity in the country, has seen delays in capacity creation, with just 1 GWh of the 40 GWh awarded installed as of March 2026. The government subsequently revised Ola Electric's timeline, allowing it to access incentives for its 20 GWh capacity through 2031. Reliance Industries, another beneficiary, has been allocated 15 GWh of capacity.

The ministry did not extend the same benefits to Bengaluru-based Rajesh Exports, which was awarded 5 GWh of capacity in 2022, citing allegations of financial misrepresentation involving around Rs.15 trillion levelled against the company by market regulator Securities and Exchange Board of India in June this year.

Another 10 GWh capacity under the scheme, earmarked for grid-scale energy storage services, is yet to be awarded. A tender for the same was floated in July.

data.title: Crude Oil Surges As U.S.-Iran Re-escalation Fears Continue To Drive Disruption Concerns
data.description:
WASHINGTON (dpa-AFX) - Rebounding from the decline in yesterday's session, crude oil prices have soared on Friday as supply disruption concerns increase. Iran is yet to respond to the U.S. call for negotiations before U.S. forces start off their planned short but intense attack on Iran by next week, as suggested by several media reports.

WTI Crude Oil for December delivery was last seen trading up by $2.39 (or 2.34%) at $104.39 per barrel.

Yesterday, the Wall Street Journal reported that U.S. Central Command Chief Admiral Brad Cooper, who is overseeing the Middle East operations, met U.S. President Donald Trump at the White House, reportedly to present the available military options against Iran.

U.S. Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth and Joint Chiefs Chairman Dan Caine were present in the meeting.

Concerns of re-escalation in the gulf region continued to accelerate.

Last Friday, the New York Times reported that the U.S. and Israel are preparing for a joint military campaign against Iran after the November 3rd U.S. mid-term elections. The operation is said to target Iran's nuclear facilities and missile and drone capabilities.

A separate open-source report tracking flights stated that more than 10 U.S. military transport aircrafts have landed at airbases in Israel.

On Monday, CNN reported that U.S. forces are readying for a big-scale attack against Iran.

On Wednesday, the Wall Street Journal reported that the U.S. military was sending a Patriot battery from Texas to strengthen its air defenses in the region.

Leaders of both nations have been sending conflicting signals on peace and war.

While Trump acknowledged ongoing talks with Iran, he also emphasized that he was doubtful if it would yield results.

In Iran, Supreme Leader Mojtaba Khamenei stated that the conditions put forth by Iran must be fulfilled for any negotiations to succeed.

Iran's Foreign Minister Abbas Araghchi remarked that while Iran is willing to allow diplomacy a chance, its army is well-prepared to combat any attack and defend the motherland.

Leadership from both sides have expressed conflicting comments over their options on war and peace.

U.S. Vice President JD Vance wrote a letter to Iran's military chief urging Iran to come to official discussions.

Reportedly, Vance wants to prevent a renewed conflict in the gulf. He also wants to persuade Trump to offer more time for diplomatic channels to achieve their goal and halt the planned attacks.

Qatar, which has been leading the mediatory efforts of the regional neighbors of Iran, with the support from Saudi Arabia, Egypt, and Turkey, is working to convince Iran to allow U.N. inspectors to visit Iran's nuclear sites.

A delegation from Qatar visited Iran on Sunday to offer a proposal and coordinate peace talks. Today, the mediatory group is visiting Iran again.

Iran's Islamic Revolutionary Guards Corps claimed that four vessels that violated Iran's protocol for shipping across the Strait of Hormuz hit sea mines planted by Iran and caught fire.

Iran is showing no tangible signs of softening its hard stance.

Iran has not spoken out on its demands or concessions it is seeking in specific terms. Further, Iran has been unresponsive to Vance's call for recommencing discussions.

Meanwhile, Yemen's Iran-backed Houthi militant group claimed a fresh series of attacks on Saudi Arabia, especially on its oil infrastructure, including two refineries (Ras Tanura and Rabigh) and a facility at the Abqaiq oil field.

Houthi Spokesperson Yahya Saree announced hitting an Aramco facility in Buqayq. The Houthis also earlier targeted Saudi airports at Dammam and Riyadh.

The U.S.-Iran war, which began in late February, has entered its ninth month. Iran closed the Strait of Hormuz for international shipping.

The modest recovery seen in oil exports, helped by alternative routes, is now under the threat of dwindling again due to the threat of an expansive war in the gulf.

Reuters reported that this month alone, WTI crude oil saw gains of around 14%.

data.title: We Drove 3,900 Miles From San Francisco to Boston With Seven Giant-Sequoia Seedlings — WSJ
data.description:
By Reporting and photography by Betsy Corcoran

Twilight was filtering through Ohio's leafy Cuyahoga Valley National Park as my husband and I parked our minivan. We then unloaded four potted seedlings onto a cart and hauled them to our campsite.

A man relaxing by a campfire watched with surprise. Who brings their own trees on a camping trip? He got even more confused when I told him what the pots were holding: giant-sequoia babies.

It was the eighth evening on a 3,900-mile road trip from California to Boston. We were delivering seven giant-sequoias babies to people who aimed to plant them in places meaningful to them. Along the way, we met many people who were both curious and charmed by the iconic conifers.

Why were we undertaking this mission? My husband and I had visited California's native sequoias during the dark days of Covid. They captured our imaginations — a sign of life and resilience in the face of a disease that made everything seem fragile and temporary. And we wanted to share the gift of that spirit with people dear to us, no matter how far we had to travel to do it.

We had made one cross-country road trip years ago, traveling east to west, young newlyweds learning about ourselves. Decades later, we were intrigued to make the journey in reverse, giving something back along the way.

Misdemeanor with a cause

Americans have been enchanted by sequoias since the 1850s, when a guy chasing a bear stumbled across the biggest tree he had ever seen. He wasn't the first to encounter them — the Yosemite Native tribes called the trees "wawona," like the sound made by the northern spotted owl. Unfortunately, early Euro-American adventurers started chopping down the gargantuan trees and shipping off chunks. It took 40 years and the combined forces of naturalist John Muir, President Benjamin Harrison and the U.S. Cavalry to set up Sequoia National Park so the trees wouldn't be logged out of existence.

More than 130 years later, in the spring of 2021, my husband, George Anders, proposed we visit Sequoia & Kings Canyon National Parks, about five hours from our California home. I figured a little "forest bathing" couldn't hurt during the pandemic.

The sequoias took my breath away. Not just because they towered overhead, the biggest dwarfing a stack of 10 blue whales. Not just because of their longevity, though their heritage dates back to the Jurassic era. Most astonishing to me were their scars: the burned-out crevices, cut deep into the heart of many of the trees, some big enough to ride a horse through. Yet the trees still thrived. Resilience is at the core of sequoias.

Rangers frown on taking even a stick from a national park. Still, I needed a reminder of these groves' peacefulness and strength. I slipped a few of the marshmallow-size Sequoia cones into my pocket.

A year later, they released seeds, which I decided to try to germinate. It worked.

Planting a tree involves touching time. You imagine a future in which the tree flourishes, providing shade and oxygen and beauty to people not yet born. That made planting a sequoia an act of radical optimism, something I hadn't felt in a long time.

Fast-forward four years: I had nurtured nine baby giant sequoias that were now outgrowing their large plastic buckets. I planted two in my tiny backyard — perhaps a bit ambitious given how large these trees could get if they survive, say, 1,000 years. (If they last even 100, they will likely outlast my house.)

But the rest of the trees? I wanted them to go to people who meant something to me.

My brother, Chris Corcoran, who lives outside Boston, loved the idea. He wanted a tree, no questions asked. His enthusiasm inspired me: Why not take a road trip, with trees? As friends heard about our evolving plans, they began raising their hands.

Spreading the roots

There were practical questions to consider, though. Was transporting trees this way legal? And was it a good idea in the first place? After all, invasive species can pose real risks to a native environment.

The answer to the first question turned out to be yes: You can take the trees across state lines, with a bit of red tape. Each plant would need a "phytosanitary certificate" attesting to compliance with the agricultural rules of its destination. The cost: about $50 apiece.

As for the potential harm: All the big environmental questions about invasive species occur when you're planting a large number of trees — hundreds or more. One tree here or there won't do much damage. Purists say you should only plant native species, but most people have something "ornamental" in their yards that is probably not native.

And, you could argue, the trees need all the help they can get. Sequoias are on the "Red List of Threatened Species" site maintained by the International Union for Conservation of Nature, along with their two cousins, coast redwoods and dawn redwoods.

"The sequoias' ancestors used to be much more widespread throughout the Northern Hemisphere," says Wendy Baxter, co-founder of the nonprofit Ancient Forest Society and a canopy scientist, who scales trees to see how they are doing. Giant-sequoia fossils have been found in Nevada, Colorado, South Dakota and other Western states. "But over time, as a result of climatic changes, their range really contracted," she says.

Baxter's organization helps create seed libraries to support reforestation. Since the 1850s, in fact, people have shared seeds and raised sequoias in places as far-flung as Scotland, France and New Zealand.

Baxter herself is a fan of growing sequoias — not really migrating whole forests, but she's fine with planting one or two. "Anything that connects people with nature and trees is a positive thing," she says.

Sequoias natively are found in small patches in California's Northern Sierra mountains, typically at elevations greater than 5,000 feet. Their thick bark helps make them especially resistant to insects and fire (which contributes to their lifespan), but they crave water. Mature sequoias, namely ones that are hundreds of years old, can consume hundreds of gallons of water a day during dry summer days.

The oldest transplanted sequoias date to the 1850s or so. The biggest of those trees is about 160 feet tall and less than 7 feet in diameter. They have done best in environments that are sunny, cooler (winter snows are fine) and, of course, near water. We did pick people who live proximate to water. And everyone promised to water the saplings faithfully while they are still small and their roots are beginning to reach out.

Have trees, will smile

Plans in place, George and I strapped our seven sequoias into a Pacifica minivan, whose 47 inches of vertical space were just enough to accommodate the tallest of our seven potted seedlings. At 8:30 a.m. on a Tuesday, we took to the road.

Traveling with trees is a bit like traveling with puppies, minus the poop bags. We overnighted in places where we could take the trees out of the van, water them and give them a couple of hours of light. Whenever we glanced in the rear view mirror, we could see the trees gently waving their tiny branches in sync with the motion of the van.

We soon discovered the best way to elicit a smile from, say, a weary convenience-store attendant or waiter was to casually mention that we were traveling with...seven. Baby. Giant. Sequoias.

Our destinations included family and friends in places as diverse as Salt Lake City, Oconomowoc, Wis., Chicago, Maryland, and the Eastern seaboard: Connecticut, Rhode Island and Massachusetts.

In Salt Lake City, one recipient, George's cousin, quickly learned that some neighbors were also raising the giant trees. "Maybe," she said, "owning a sequoia is like walking a dog. It introduces you to all sorts of people you might not meet otherwise."

Six days into the journey, the arid dryness of the West yielded to the extravagant green of the Great Lakes states, where we delivered a sequoia to our niece in Oconomowoc and to a friend who plans to plant his sequoia next spring in northern Michigan. Our niece and her husband have a toddler who is nearly 2 years old; raising a giant sequoia didn't seem scarier than trying to raise a child. Our friend with plans for Michigan loved the long view: "What appeals to me is the length of the project. Thirty years, 40 — or a thousand, for a Sequoia! It's like touching immortality."

Next came the Maryland shore, to see my long-ago boss and his wife. For years, he has planted White Oaks acorns each year, a tradition he started years ago when his family owned Virginia farmland. The oldest of those trees are now 30 feet high. Over time, he has added maples, redbuds and others, which have become gifts for family and friends. I liked to think of us adding to this horticultural community.

A special homecoming

In the final leg of our journey, we headed up the East Coast to deliver the last three sequoias. First up is my hometown, Newtown, Conn., where my best friend has retired with her husband. Bringing a sequoia to Newtown — site of the Sandy Hook attack on schoolchildren — resonates deeply. I'm not sure anyone in Newtown will ever fully recover from the aftermath of that brutal assault. But the town, like a sequoia, carries on.

Another tree went to friends in Providence — archaeologists who, as one said, take the long view and are good at digging. Perfect for sequoias. Finally, we reached our last destination, the one that got the trip rolling in the first place: Concord, Mass., home to Thoreau's Walden Pond and the bridge where the first shots of the Revolution were fired. My brother and his wife live in a wooded section of town, where a dawn redwood is already flourishing on their property.

data.title: Cruise Stocks Had a Great Week. They Can Keep Steaming Ahead. — Barrons.com
data.description:
By Teresa Rivas

Investors were treating cruise stocks like sinking ships in late summer. But the latest earnings results show travelers haven't given up on seaborne vacations, and analysts see gains ahead for the stocks.

Both Royal Caribbean Group and Norwegian Cruise Line Holdings delivered third-quarter results ahead of expectations this week, coming on the heels of Carnival Corp.'s robust report in late September.

Investors had been concerned about cruise lines in general because of the energy price spike: Not only do ships require oodles of fuel, but higher gasoline prices crimp consumers' discretionary budgets. The underlying cause of energy inflation, the Iran war, was a worry in itself in terms of some sailing itineraries, while historically low levels in European rivers also hurt Viking Holdings' stock, as it's known for its river cruises on the continent.

A hantavirus outbreak earlier this year didn't help the industry either.

But this week's crop of results show that despite concerns about the industry, demand remains strong.

Travel in general has proven resilient — United Airlines highlighted total revenue per available seat-mile grew at its highest quarterly rate since the pandemic when it reported last week, while Marriott stock notched its longest winning streak since 2019 earlier this month.

Cruises can sometimes provide better value than land-based vacations, which makes them a better option for budget-conscious travelers, and easily accommodate multigenerational trips — a key advantage when grandparents are increasingly footing the bill.

Royal Caribbean is the favorite of the three major cruise lines and it's not hard to see why: It's the only one trading above its prepandemic share price, has been a consistent performer, and Wall Street is warming to its investment in Sandals.

"While 2026 has had its fair share of curveballs, Royal is still poised to grow earnings per share by about 14%," wrote William Blair analyst Sharon Zackfia, explaining her bullish stance on the stock after this week's earnings. "[S]tructural factors will continue driving healthy growth including...a bigger and deeper competitive moat from past and future investments in industry-leading innovative ships and owned destinations."

Norwegian hasn't fared as well, but even skeptics like Truist Securities analyst C. Patrick Scholes, who's sidelined on the stock, saw clear positives, particularly in the company's 2027 net yield guidance (used to measure pricing power, as excludes variable costs like commissions and transportation). Norwegian expects the metric to grow between 1% and 2%, slightly above the 0.9% consensus estimate, and "it has been a long time since nearly any type of guide at earnings for Norwegian has been better than consensus expectations," he writes.

All three major cruise line stocks, along with Viking, are up for the week thanks to the post-earnings bumps.

Although oil will remain an overhang as long as prices remain elevated, at least this might put to rest some worries that have acted like an anchor on the group.

Write to Teresa Rivas at teresa.rivas@barrons.com

data.title: Canadian dollar extends monthly gain as higher oil prices raise inflation risk
data.description:
By Fergal Smith

The Canadian dollar strengthened to a six-week high against its US counterpart on Friday as a jump in oil prices supported bets the Bank of Canada would tighten further, overshadowing disappointing GDP data.

The loonie was trading 0.2% higher at 1.3955 per US dollar, or 71.66 US cents, after touching its strongest intraday level since September 16 at 1.3943. For the month, the currency was on track to gain 2%, which would be its biggest monthly advance since April.

  • Canada's economy stalled in August for the second straight month, while advance estimates showed GDP declining 0.1% in September and annualized third-quarter growth of 1.3%. The BoC has projected the economy growing by 2% in the third quarter.

  • "Markets ignored Canadian GDP and with good reason," Derek Holt, head of capital markets economics at Scotiabank, said in a note.

  • "While the figures disappointed somewhat, the BoC is forward-looking and focused upon rising inflation risk that has many complex drivers — like oil that is fired up this morning," Holt said.

  • On Wednesday, the Bank of Canada hiked its key interest rate by 25 basis points to 2.50% and said further increases might be needed to prevent soaring energy costs from driving broader inflation.

  • Investors see a roughly 50% chance the central bank tightens at its next policy decision in December and have fully discounted a move by January. (0#CADIRPR)

  • US crude oil futures were trading 2.7% higher at $104.80 a barrel as traders braced for a potential escalation in the US-Iran conflict after the US midterm elections. Oil is one of Canada's major exports.

  • Canadian bond yields eased across a steeper curve as a sharp selloff in technology-related stocks pushed investors into safe-haven assets such as US Treasuries.

  • The 10-year (CA10YT=RR) was down 2.1 basis points at 3.780%, after earlier touching its lowest level since September 4 at 3.768%.

data.title: Apple Stocks Edge Lower With Supply Limits Setting the Earnings Bar
data.description:
Apple , the iPhone maker and services provider, faces a simple earnings test: turn demand into revenue despite supply limits. Shares moved lower 0.55% to $346.99 at 12:35 p.m. ET on October 30. An AD HOC NEWS preview puts the reporting date at November 2, setting up a checkpoint for September-quarter sales and the production capacity behind them. Strong customer interest could offer little comfort if Apple cannot deliver enough devices.

Apple's July earnings release reported June-quarter revenue of $109.4 billion, up 16%. Reuters' July 30 coverage put management's September-quarter revenue growth guidance at 9%11%, with supply and currency constraints weighing on the outlook. That midpoint implies a six-percentage-point slowdown from June's growth rate. The key question is what drove the moderation: limited availability, softer demand, or a combination of both. June's revenue provides context, while September's year-earlier results supply the relevant comparison.

The valuation leaves Apple with plenty to prove. GuruFocus shows a GF Score of 95 out of 100, with profitability and growth standing out, while financial strength and valuation score less strongly on the displayed radar. At 39.78 times earnings and a $5.06 trillion market value, investors are paying a substantial premium for that business quality. The holiday-quarter outlook could therefore carry as much weight as September's results: Apple needs to show that component availability and production capacity can support demand and sustain growth.
